Elizabeth Loftus

American psychologist. Her experiments showed that memories can be altered by later information, with direct consequences for trials and eyewitness testimony.

Biography

Elizabeth Loftus was born in Los Angeles in 1944. She studied mathematics and psychology and earned her doctorate at Stanford in 1970. After early work on semantic memory, she became interested in something closer to real life: what witnesses to an accident or a crime remember. She has worked at the University of Washington and, since 2002, at the University of California, Irvine.

Questions she investigated

  • Can a question change what someone remembers seeing?
  • Is it possible to remember in detail something that never happened?
  • What should judges and juries know about witness memory?

Contributions

In a 1974 experiment with John Palmer, several groups watched the same film of a car crash. When the question used the verb "smashed" instead of "contacted", speed estimates were higher; a week later, more people in the first group said they had seen broken glass, which was not in the film. This is the misinformation effect.

In the 1990s, with the study known as "lost in the mall", she showed that some participants came to remember, fully or partly, an invented childhood episode when relatives presented it as real. Her work has influenced how line-ups and police interviews are conducted.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

Her research continues Frederic Bartlett's idea that remembering is reconstructing. She has served as an expert witness in hundreds of trials and was a central voice in the 1990s debates about "recovered memories" in therapy.

Criticism, limits and reception

Some critics have questioned how far laboratory experiments generalise to real traumatic memories, and her role in high-profile court cases has been controversial. The ethics of inducing false memories have also been debated. That memory is malleable does not mean all memories are false: it means they need corroborating.

References

  1. Loftus, E. F. y Palmer, J. C. (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 13(5), 585–589.
  2. Loftus, E. F. y Pickrell, J. E. (1995). The formation of false memories. Psychiatric Annals, 25(12), 720–725.
  3. Loftus, E. F. (2005). Planting misinformation in the human mind. Learning & Memory, 12(4), 361–366.
